title: Damping, forced oscillations and resonance; Rutherford scattering and atomic models
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: Q06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; Q06-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; O04-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; Q06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: O04-uk1#N.3, Q06-1#N.4, O04-uk1#N.5, Q06-1#N.7a, O04-uk1#N.10, Q06-1#N.14a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nucleus
items.clue: Tiny positive core holding over 99.9% of the mass of an atom.

items.label: Neutron
items.clue: Particle found with protons in the tiny positive core; discovered in 1932.

items.label: Light damping
items.clue: Condition in which the amplitude falls by roughly the same fraction on every cycle.

items.label: Electron
items.clue: Particle held around the positive core by its attraction; about 1/1840 of the mass of a proton.

questions.stem: A lightly damped mass–spring system is released with an amplitude of 60 mm. After one complete oscillation its amplitude is 45 mm. The amplitude falls by the same fraction in each oscillation. What is the amplitude after three complete oscillations?
questions.explanation: Each amplitude is 0.75 × the previous one: 60 × 0.75³ = 25 mm.

questions.stem: Predict first. Which statement about the results of the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford alpha-particle scattering experiment is correct?

options.text: Most of the alpha particles were deflected through large angles, and only a few passed straight through.
Nearly all the alpha particles passed through almost undeflected; a very few were deflected by more than 90°.
The few alpha particles that bounced back had collided with the electrons in the gold atoms.
The few alpha particles that bounced back had struck the hard outer surface of a gold nucleus.

questions.stem: Damping reduces the amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator from 40 mm to 20 mm. What fraction of the original oscillation energy has been transferred to the surroundings?

options.text: None, because the period has not changed

questions.explanation: E ∝ A². Half the amplitude leaves 1/4 of the energy, so 3/4 has been transferred to the surroundings.

questions.stem: A gold nucleus has radius 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and a gold atom has radius 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Roughly what fraction of the atom's volume does the nucleus occupy?
questions.explanation: (7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰)³ = (5.0 × 10⁻⁵)³ = 1.25 × 10⁻¹³. The atom is almost entirely empty space.

questions.stem: A car's wing mirror buzzes violently at one engine speed. A rubber damper is fitted to the mirror's mounting. What happens now as the engine passes that speed?

options.text: The violent buzzing moves to a much higher engine speed.
The mirror stops responding to the engine at all.
It still buzzes most near the same engine speed, but far less.
It now buzzes strongly at every engine speed.

questions.explanation: Damping removes energy every cycle. The resonance peak stays at about the same frequency but is much lower (and broader).

questions.stem: A gold nucleus is about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m across and a gold atom is about 2.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ m across. In a scale drawing the nucleus is a dot 1 mm across. How wide must the atom be drawn?
